I try really hard not to read minds, so I'll share what goes on in my own brain:

When I hear conspiracy theories, when they're worded in a way that makes it sound like there's a plan, I have this vision of the Skull & Bones or Bilderberg Society or whatever with giant whiteboards planning that in 2032 this person will become President so that in 2048 this other person can be President and pass a law on management of proles or whatever. I suspect that's what a lot of critics of "conspiracy theories" picture.

What I believe is that there are natural forces that work as the result of human nature - the uber-rich are uber-rich because they are fixated on amassing money. This desire isn't abated when they get a certain amount, so they keep wanting more, which gets a lot easier when you've got more money to work with.

So various wealthy people in various positions do things to help themselves make more money: get a lobbyist to push for a change in credit regulation; another gets a lobbyist to push for a change in taxes so they get a new loophole, and so on. Since all these little forces are driven by people with money to get more money, they all operate to move money from the general population to a small group of folks who have the money to pay lobbyists.

Similarly, each appointed official in the government has a job they envision as important. In the pursuit of this job, there will be limits on their authority that confounds their ability to do their job - like a little piece of ice poking into the tobaggan run. So they want to chip off that one piece of ice. Multiply that by legions of appointed officials and add in elected officials and again you get all these little forces that operate together to erode rights and increase the authority of the government.

It's not a design - it's an effect.

No appointed official ever comes to work and thinks "Hey, my calendar is pretty light today. I should review all these regulations and see which ones I can get rid of." Both because it's inventing work and because nobody wants to be the guy who lobbied to get rid of a police power the month before that police power would have prevented a terrorist attack. (Imagine if a guy at the FAA had gotten some kind of background check for pilots' licenses eliminated in 2000)

Increasing government power and eroding rights are like ratchets - with pressure, they tick one click tighter, but they never go back. Click... click... click...

That's why the next Constitutional Amendment I want is "All laws passed by Congress shall expire 20 years from the date of enactment into law. All existing laws will expire on the decade anniversary of their passage. No law may be re-enacted - the full text must be passed by both houses as a new law." (and have it include executive orders, administrative regulations, etc)

Nothing is more amazing than watching a law with a sunset provision fail to be renewed.
